nameStory: The Parasitic Jaeger earned its name from its thieving lifestyle — it's a master pirate of the skies! These aggressive seabirds specialize in kleptoparasitism, which means they chase and harass other birds until they drop or regurgitate their freshly caught fish, then swoop in to steal the meal. Think of them as the ocean's bullies, living up to their parasitic reputation by making other birds do the hard work of fishing.
description: The Parasitic Jaeger is a sleek, gull-like seabird with a pirate's attitude and the flying skills to match. About the size of a large gull, these birds have long, pointed wings built for high-speed aerial chases and sharp, hooked bills perfect for grabbing stolen fish. They come in two main color forms — a light phase with white underparts and a dark phase that's chocolate brown all over. These Arctic breeders pass through New England waters during migration, bringing their aggressive feeding behavior to our coastal areas.

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Flies with quick, powerful wingbeats and incredible agility — watch for dramatic high-speed chases as they pursue other seabirds, twisting and turning through the air like an aerial dogfight

idTips.label: Tail Shape
idTips.description: Adult birds show distinctive pointed central tail feathers that extend beyond the rest of the tail, creating a spear-like projection that's visible even at a distance

idTips.label: Bill and Legs
idTips.description: Dark, sharply hooked bill with a slight bulge at the tip, paired with blackish legs — the bill feels substantial and predatory compared to a gull's more generalized beak

idTips.label: Body Build
idTips.description: More compact and muscular than gulls, with a barrel-chested appearance and longer, more pointed wings that give them a falcon-like silhouette in flight

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Relentlessly chases terns, gulls, and other seabirds until they drop their catch — this harassment behavior is so persistent it looks almost comical, like a schoolyard bully demanding lunch money

idTips.label: Color Variations
idTips.description: Appears in light phase (white belly, dark cap and back) or dark phase (uniform chocolate-brown), with many intermediate forms showing varying amounts of barring on the underparts

habitat: Look for Parasitic Jaegers in New England's offshore waters, particularly around fishing areas where other seabirds concentrate. They're most often spotted from ferries, whale-watching boats, or prominent coastal headlands during migration periods. These birds prefer open ocean environments but will venture closer to shore when following flocks of terns and gulls that they can rob of fish.

seasonality.spring: Parasitic Jaegers begin passing through New England waters in late spring, often seen chasing terns that are actively fishing. Look for their aggressive aerial pursuits during May and early June.
seasonality.summer: Peak migration continues through summer months, with birds in breeding plumage showing their most distinct tail projections and clearest color patterns as they head to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings the highest numbers through New England waters from August through October, including many juveniles that lack the long tail feathers of adults.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in winter as these birds continue south to warmer waters across the southern hemisphere, though occasional stragglers may linger in offshore areas.

funFact: Parasitic Jaegers are so specialized at aerial piracy that they can force a tern to regurgitate its fish, then catch the falling meal in mid-air before it hits the water — sometimes accomplishing this incredible feat while both birds are flying at full speed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with gulls at first glance, but their aggressive chase behavior is a dead giveaway — gulls don't typically engage in the relentless aerial harassment that defines jaegers. Remember: if you see a gull-like bird bullying other seabirds in dramatic aerial chases, you're watching a jaeger!
contextualKnowledge: The terms "jaeger" and "skua" refer to the same family of birds, with "jaeger" (meaning "hunter" in German) used in North America and "skua" more common in Europe. This can cause confusion when reading field guides from different regions, but they're describing the same group of piratical seabirds.
compareHints: Parasitic Jaegers are intermediate in size between the smaller Long-tailed Jaeger and the bulkier Pomarine Jaeger. They lack the Long-tailed's extremely elongated, flexible tail streamers and the Pomarine's distinctive spoon-shaped tail projections and heavier build. The Parasitic Jaeger's pointed but moderate tail extensions and medium build make it the "goldilocks" of the jaeger family — not too big, not too small, but just right for aggressive aerial piracy.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pomarine Jaegers are the bulkiest of the three regular jaeger species in New England waters, noticeably stockier than the slender Long-tailed Jaeger and chunkier than the Parasitic Jaeger.
Among the three jaeger species found in New England waters, the Long-tailed is the smallest and most delicate, with the most pronounced tail streamers when adult.
Unlike the smaller jaegers in its family, South Polar Skua has a much heavier build and shorter, squared tail rather than the elongated central tail feathers of adult jaegers.
Great Skuas are much larger and more robust than their jaeger relatives (Parasitic, Pomarine, and Long-tailed Jaegers).
